title: Redwood edgecases demo: long context / high TPS / streaming/backpressure/timeouts
summary: Redwood AE+SE ran an edge-cases demo focusing on long-context (>200k token) ingestion, high TPS bursts (target 1.5-2k tps), and streaming backpressure/timeouts. Customer expressed concerns about tail latency, graceful degradation, and VPC/on-prem options for PHI. Agreed next steps: share pricing and security pack, run pilot benchmark with customer prompts, and schedule infra deep-dive with SREs.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-02
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Reyes (CTO - Nimbus HealthTech), Priya Kapoor (Eng Manager), Lee Wong (SRE)

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick agenda, we'll run through four main edge cases - long context, high TPS, streaming/backpressure behavior, and how timeouts are handled. Samir will demo the Console and Optimize suggestions.
[00:30] Jordan: Yep, excited. For context, our product indexes patient history PDFs and needs to keep really long context windows, sometimes >100k tokens, looking to push to 200k in a pilot. Also expected bursts up to 1.5k to 2k TPS for summary endpoints.
[00:50] Priya: And on SEC/compliance side, we need SOC2, KMS, and VPC support because PHI is involved. Also low tail latency is critical for triage flows.
[01:10] Alex: Totally. We'll show both hosted and Dedicated approaches and the Private (VPC) options. Samir, can you start the console demo?
[01:25] Samir: Sure, pulling up the Console. Quick note, transcript may show some model names wrong - the demo uses our 8B-quant and a 70B-quant fallback for high latency cases.
[01:40] Samir: (shares screen) Here in Optimize you'll see batching, cache TTLs, and quantization profiles. For long context we use chunked KV caching and prefix-only caching by default to avoid full KV blowup.
[02:05] Jordan: When you say "chunked KV" do you mean you shard the KV cache across requests or across GPUs? I.e., how do you avoid OOM for a 200k token KV?
[02:20] Samir: Good question. We shard the KV across the serving pool and use checkpointed KV eviction - older prefixes are snapshotted to a low-latency cold store. It's a hybrid approach; sorry if the transcription says "KV cash" earlier, it's KV cache.
[02:40] Lee: Sounds like some of that will need private connectivity. If you snapshot to an external store, we need to ensure it's inside our VPC or under our KMS.
[02:55] Alex: We support a Private deployment where the snapshot store can be customer-hosted or behind a VPC peering, and KMS integration for envelope encryption. We'll share the security pack after this call.
[03:15] Jordan: Walk me through the TPS side. If I spike to 2k TPS with 512-token responses, what happens?
[03:30] Samir: There are a few levers: autoscaling (Dedicated), request routing to lower-cost variants for non-critical paths, and continuous batching. For 2k TPS we recommend Dedicated pools with pre-warmed burst capacity and autoscale thresholds tuned.
[03:50] Priya: What's the typical latency at tail for Dedicated with pre-warmed? Our SLO is 150ms p95 for short responses.
[04:05] Samir: For short responses (<=256 tokens) on Dedicated with NVLink-enabled nodes, p95 can be under 120ms in our benchmarks. At 2k TPS those numbers depend on seq-length distribution and batching strategy - we'll run a benchmark with your actual workload.
[04:30] Jordan: Okay, demo the streaming scenario where the client disconnects mid-stream and how Redwood handles backpressure/timeouts.
[04:45] Samir: Switching to streaming demo. Let's open a high-TPS streaming test harness... (typing) Sending continuous stream requests with artificially slowed client ack to model backpressure.
[05:10] Samir: [05:10] Server emits chunk, client ack delayed, runtime's backpressure algorithm detects slow consumer and applies windowing - we pause the kernel but keep KV preserved; after a threshold we start graceful degradation: reduce max tokens or switch to a lower-latency model variant to avoid full request timeouts.
[05:40] Lee: So you don't outright drop connections? We need guaranteed delivery for certain flows.
[05:50] Samir: We try not to drop. There's a configurable policy: block-until-ack for critical flows, or best-effort fallback where we return a partial result plus a continuation token for the client to fetch remaining context.
[06:15] Priya: That continuation token approach—how is state stored? Is it a reference we host or we hand a resumable prompt back to the client?
[06:28] Samir: It's a hosted resumable token by default (opaque id referencing KV snapshot). For Private deployments you can control that store. Opaque token TTLs and access are enforced by RBAC and can be KMS encrypted.
[06:45] Jordan: Any real-world numbers on timeouts? We saw some providers time out during 30-second windows when bursty clients applied backpressure.
[07:00] Samir: In our stress tests we tune the grace window to trade latency vs memory. For 2k TPS with 1% slow clients, we saw single-digit percent increases in tail latency if fallback policies are enabled; without fallbacks, timeouts and retries spike and cost explodes. We'll show the test plan.
[07:30] Alex: Quick interruption — competitors? Jordan, you mentioned evaluating Anthropic and OpenAI. Any others?
[07:40] Jordan: DepthAI was on the RFP. Key differences we care about are pricing predictability and private deployment options.
[07:55] Alex: Noted. Samir, can you run a short live pipeline to show a 100k token ingest and a long-context retrieval?
[08:05] Samir: Running now. Uploading a synthetic 120k-token doc, indexing, then querying for a 1k token summary. (typing sounds)
[08:30] Samir: [08:30] Ok upload done. The index step uses chunking and semantic compression, see console -> Optimize suggests 8-16 token chunk overlaps and long-term embeddings to speed retrieval.
[08:52] Priya: What's the RAM footprint per 100k token document? Our infra budget won't allow huge per-doc memory.
[09:05] Samir: With semantic compression we reduce active KV by ~60% in typical docs; exact numbers depend on model and chunk size. For 120k tokens it's still non-trivial — for that we recommend hybrid: keep hot segments in memory, cold prefix on disk. That's configurable per route.
[09:30] Lee: And for encryption in transit and at rest? KMS?
[09:40] Alex: We support TLS in transit and envelope encryption at rest; KMS integration for customer-managed keys is available on Private and Dedicated with extra guardrails. We'll attach the KMS playbook in the security pack.
[09:55] Jordan: Anything around audit logs? We need request-level logs for any access to PHI.
[10:05] Alex: Console has token-level audit logs and per-route tracing; logs can be forwarded to your SIEM or retained per your retention policy.
[10:20] Samir: Back to streaming: I'll simulate a client that acks irregularly which forces backpressure. (typing) Sending 200 concurrent streams, ramping to 1k TPS, then inject 50 slow clients.
[11:00] Samir: [11:00] You can see in the trace that the runtime starts applying windowing at t+3s and we start model-variant fallback at t+7s. The client sees smaller chunks sooner; we emit a continuation token in the event of truncation.
[11:25] Priya: If we get partial results, can we request resume later with the token and get deterministic output? We require deterministic resumability.
[11:35] Samir: Determinism is hard with non-deterministic sampling; for resumability we provide two modes: deterministic (use sampling=0 / greedy + cached KV) or probabilistic with checkpointed latent state. We recommend deterministic mode for regulatory flows.
[12:00] Jordan: How about cost? If we use deterministic resumability, that can increase token cost, right?
[12:10] Alex: It can. That's where Optimize helps — we show cost vs quality trade-offs in the console and give recommendations, e.g., quantize to 4-bit for non-critical passes and use higher-precision for final responses.
[12:30] Jordan: We wanted to see the rollback/fallback policy in action too — can you demo A/B or canary where traffic gets routed to a cheaper variant on overload?
[12:45] Samir: Yep. In Routing we configure priority pools: primary equals 70B-quant, fallback 8B-quant. On overload policy is - route 20% to fallback, then 50% then full if overload persists. This prevents full outage.
[13:10] Lee: From SRE perspective, what's observable? We need per-token latency, queue depth, and memory per-gpu metrics exported.
[13:25] Samir: All exposed via tracing hooks and Prometheus metrics; Console gives a per-route dashboard, and we can forward to your Grafana.
[13:40] Priya: For pilot scope, we want to reproduce our worst-case: 200k token ingest + peak 1.5k TPS with 5% slow clients. Can Redwood run that benchmark for us?
[13:55] Samir: Yes, we'll need your sample dataset and a simple harness script. We'll provide our benchmark harness and a ramp profile.
[14:10] Alex: Next steps we'll send the harness and an initial quote for Dedicated pre-warm capacity.
[14:20] Jordan: On contracts, what SLAs do you offer for Dedicated pools?
[14:30] Alex: SLA depends on tier. For enterprise Dedicated we have 99.95% uptime with latency SLOs and credits for breaches. We'll include SLA language in the enterprise pack.
[14:45] Priya: One more thing — network egress costs. If you do snapshotting to a cold store outside our cloud account, that could be a surprise.
[14:55] Alex: We'll note that in the proposal — Private deployments avoid cross-account egress; for hosted snapshots we document egress assumptions.
[15:10] Samir: Running a quick stress log now to show timeout behavior in the trace... (pause) you can see a few edge cases where client disconnect triggers a best-effort response. There are some garbled words in the auto transcript here, it says "streaming timeouts are sexier" which is nonsense.
[15:35] Jordan: (laughs) Alright. What about durability of continuation tokens? If the token references an in-memory KV and we evict it, do you guarantee rehydration?
[15:50] Samir: Continuation tokens reference a snapshot which lives in the low-latency cold store for a configurable TTL; if the snapshot expired we return a 410 and the client must re-run or fetch a shorter context. For critical flows you can raise TTL or pin the snapshot.
[16:15] Lee: Pinning sounds expensive — what's the cost model for pinned snapshots?
[16:25] Alex: Pinned snapshots are meterable - we bill based on storage retention and access patterns; we'll include price examples in the SKU.
[16:40] Priya: Any limitations on sequence length for the 70B fallback? Do you truncate or use sliding windows?
[16:50] Samir: For large seqs we use sliding windows with overlap tuning and semantic compression; the model itself isn't limited arbitrarily but memory and latency dictate practical caps.
[17:05] Jordan: Quick question about telemetry for the pilot — can you tag traces with our customer_id and route names for cross-correlation?
[17:15] Samir: Yes, we support request-level metadata and custom tags; we can add a header for customer_id.
[17:30] Alex: Okay wrapping up — recap of next steps: pricing, security docs, benchmark harness, schedule SRE deep-dive. Anything else?
[17:45] Jordan: Please include a cost estimate for deterministic resumable mode vs probabilistic.
[17:55] Alex: Will do.
[18:05] Priya: And can we get a short doc on recommended route configs for long-context retrieval?
[18:12] Samir: I'll attach a sample route config + Optimize profile.
[18:20] Lee: We'll aim to get you a sample dataset by Monday.
[18:30] Alex: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email with links and the security pack.
[18:40] Jordan: Thanks all.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription quality: speaker labels sometimes generic; a few medical acronyms were mistranscribed (PHI -> FHI). The content retains filler and stutters.
